claim: The whale shark genome assembly had 57,333 contigs with a contig N50 of 144,422 bp.
source: The new assembly had 57,333 contigs with a contig N50 of 144,422 bp, or fewer contigs than the number of scaffolds of previous assemblies, and a higher contig N50, representing a dramatic improvement in gapless contiguity compared to the existing whale shark genome assemblies (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly reports assembly statistics from the sequencing and assembly process.

claim: The whale shark genome assembly has higher contig contiguity than all other cartilaginous fish genomes.
source: This higher contiguity at the contig level (vs. scaffold level) was also better than the published Callorhinchus, brownbanded bamboo shark, cloudy catshark, and white shark genomes (Hara et al., 2018; Marra et al., 2019; Venkatesh et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript compares assembly statistics to previously published cartilaginous fish genomes.

claim: The total length of the new whale shark genome assembly was 2.96 Gbp.
source: The total length of the new assembly was 2.96 Gbp.
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the total assembly length.

claim: The whale shark genome size estimated from k-mer-based approach GenomeScope was approximately 2.79 Gbp.
source: The total size of the assembly was very similar to the genome size estimated from the k-mer-based approach GenomeScope of ~2.79 Gbp, suggesting the genome is fairly complete.
evidence: The manuscript reports genome size estimation using GenomeScope.

claim: The whale shark genome assembly is smaller than the non-sequencing-based estimate of 3.73 Gbp by Hara et al., 2018.
source: On the other hand, it was smaller than a non-sequencing-based estimate of the whale shark genome size of 3.73 Gbp by Hara et al., 2018, which suggests that sections of the genome, potentially comprising primarily repetitive elements, are still missing.
evidence: The manuscript compares the assembly size to a previously published estimate.

claim: Repetitive elements comprise roughly 50.34% of the whale shark genome assembly.
source: Repetitive elements were annotated to comprise roughly 50.34% of the genome assembly (Appendix 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of repetitive elements from annotation.

claim: The whale shark genome had an estimated level of heterozygosity of approximately 0.0797–0.0828%.
source: Based on GenomeScope, the whale shark genome had an estimated level of heterozygosity of ~0.0797–0.0828%, consistent with the k-mer coverage plot showing a unimodal distribution (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports heterozygosity estimates from GenomeScope analysis.

claim: SNP calling using freebayes provided an estimate of 2,189,244 SNPs, a rate of 0.0739% heterozygosity.
source: Mapping the reads to the genome assembly and calling SNPs using freebayes provided a similar estimate of 2,189,244 SNPs, a rate of 0.0739% heterozygosity, or an average of an SNP every 1353 bases.
evidence: The manuscript reports SNP counts and heterozygosity rate from freebayes analysis.

claim: The heterozygosity of the whale shark genome is relatively low.
source: This suggests that the heterozygosity of the whale shark genome is relatively low.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the heterozygosity data.

claim: BUSCO v2 found 2033 complete orthologs in the whale shark genome, of which 1967 were single-copy and 66 had duplicates.
source: Of 2586 orthologs conserved among vertebrates searched by BUSCO (Simão et al., 2015), we found 2033 complete orthologs in the whale shark genome, of which 1967 were single-copy and 66 had duplicates; 323 orthologs were detected as fragments, while 230 were not detected by BUSCO.
evidence: The manuscript reports BUSCO completeness statistics.

claim: The whale shark genome has 78.7% complete BUSCO genes, representing a marked improvement over the previous whale shark genome assembly which only had 15% complete BUSCO genes.
source: With 78.7% complete genes, this represents a marked improvement over the previous whale shark genome assembly, which only had 15% complete BUSCO genes (Hara et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript compares BUSCO completeness to a previous assembly.

claim: Using the CVG set, 85% of CVGs were complete and 97.4% of CVGs included partial genes in the whale shark genome.
source: We also evaluated gene completeness using a rigid one-to-one ortholog core vertebrate gene (CVG) set that is better tuned for finding gene families in elasmobranchs (Hara et al., 2015) implemented in gVolante server (Nishimura et al., 2017; Nishimura et al., 2019), we found that 85% of CVGs were complete and found that 97.4% of CVGs included partial genes, which compares favorably to completeness statistics in other shark assemblies (Hara et al., 2018; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports CVG completeness statistics.

claim: Genes from 37 chordate species were assigned to 18,435 orthologous gene families using OrthoFinder.
source: Genes from the proteomes for 37 chordate species deriving primarily from Ensembl and RefSeq (O'Leary et al., 2016; Yates et al., 2020; Supplementary file 3), including 35 representative vertebrates, a sea squirt (Ciona), and a lancelet (Branchiostoma) were assigned to 18,435 orthologous gene families using OrthoFinder, which were assigned to a mean of 10,688 orthogroups per genome (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of orthogroups identified by OrthoFinder.

claim: There was a major increase in gene families at the origin of gnathostomes (jawed vertebrates) independent of their genome duplication.
source: We found a major increase in gene families at the origin of gnathostomes (jawed vertebrates) independent of their genome duplication.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding in the abstract.

claim: There was a consistent increase in the total number of gene families from the root to the MRCA of Gnathostomata, but only slight increases following this in the MRCAs of bony fishes and cartilaginous fishes.
source: We inferred a consistent increase in the total number of gene families from the root to the MRCA of Gnathostomata, but only slight increases following this in the MRCAs of bony fishes and cartilaginous fishes (black numbers, Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports gene family evolution patterns with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Novel gene families increased from the root to a peak in the MRCA of gnathostomes, and then novelty decreased precipitously toward the bony and cartilaginous fish descendants.
source: We also found numbers of novel gene families increased from the root to a peak in the MRCA of gnathostomes, and then novelty decreased precipitously toward the bony and cartilaginous fish descendants (numbers indicated by + symbol, Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports gene family novelty patterns with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The origin of jawed vertebrates established a large proportion of novel gene families of both bony vertebrates and cartilaginous fishes, with variable retention among descendant lineages.
source: Overall, this implied that the origin of jawed vertebrates established a large proportion of novel gene families of both bony vertebrates and cartilaginous fishes, with variable retention among descendant lineages.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the gene family evolution data.

claim: Only 157 (5.4% of 2885 gene families) of gene families inferred to have originated in the MRCA of jawed vertebrates corresponded to split ohnologs.
source: We found that only 157 (5.4% of 2885 gene families) of gene families that we inferred to have originated in the MRCA of jawed vertebrates corresponded to split ohnologs.
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of gene families that are split ohnologs.

claim: Only three gene families were inferred to be derived at the MRCA of teleosts, coinciding with the teleost-specific genome duplication.
source: In addition, we also found that only three gene families were inferred to be derived at the MRCA of teleosts, coinciding with the teleost-specific genome duplication, which also supports that gene family inference is robust to genome duplication.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of gene families derived at the MRCA of teleosts.

claim: For the 711 novel gene families in the MRCA of Olfactores, there was an enrichment of connexin function.
source: For example, for the 711 novel gene families in the MRCA of Olfactores, we found an enrichment of connexin function (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The manuscript reports functional enrichment analysis results.

claim: The origin of connexin gap junction proteins among chordates was in the MRCA in Olfactores.
source: This is consistent with prior work that determined that the origin of connexin gap junction proteins among chordates was in the MRCA in Olfactores (Alexopoulos et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on connexin origins.

claim: Among the novel proteins in the MRCA of vertebrates, there was enrichment of several protein domain types including rhodopsin family 7-transmembrane (7-TM) receptor domains, immunoglobulin V-set domain, collagen triple helix repeats, zona pellucida domain, and C2H2-type zinc finger domain.
source: Among the novel proteins in the MRCA of vertebrates, we found enrichment of several protein domain types including rhodopsin family 7-transmembrane (7-TM) receptor domains, immunoglobulin V-set domain, collagen triple helix repeats, zona pellucida domain, and C2H2-type zinc finger domain (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: The manuscript reports functional enrichment analysis results for vertebrate ancestor.

claim: The enrichment of collagen function is consistent with the importance of these collagens at the origin of vertebrates and their potential involvement in origin of vertebrate traits, such as bone and teeth.
source: The enrichment of collagen function is consistent with the importance of these collagens at the origin of vertebrates and their potential involvement in origin of vertebrate traits, such as bone and teeth (Boot-Handford and Tuckwell, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the collagen enrichment finding with reference to prior work.

claim: Zona pellucida proteins likely originated in vertebrates.
source: The enrichment of the zona pellucida domain at the origin of vertebrates is consistent with previous evidence showing that zona pellucida proteins likely originated in vertebrates (Litscher and Wassarman, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on zona pellucida protein origins.

claim: In the MRCA of jawed vertebrates, there was enrichment of a variety of immune-related protein domains including immunoglobulin V-set domain, immunoglobulin C1-set domain, and interleukin-8-like small cytokines, with functional enrichment of immune response and hormone activity.
source: In the MRCA of jawed vertebrates, we found enrichment of a variety of immune-related protein domains including immunoglobulin V-set domain, immunoglobulin C1-set domain, and interleukin-8-like small cytokines, with functional enrichment of immune response and hormone activity.
evidence: The manuscript reports functional enrichment analysis results for jawed vertebrate ancestor.

claim: Immunoglobulin domain containing gene families included many immunoglobulins, interleukins, interleukin receptors, T-cell receptors, sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-type lectins (Siglec proteins), chemokines, cluster of differentiation (CD) proteins, and MHC proteins.
source: Immunoglobulin domain containing gene families included many immunoglobulins, interleukins, interleukin receptors, T-cell receptors, sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-type lectins (Siglec proteins), chemokines, cluster of differentiation (CD) proteins, and MHC proteins (Supplementary file 9), consistent with the evolution of immunoglobulin/T-cell receptor-based adaptive immunity in gnathostomes (Boehm, 2012; Kaiser et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript lists gene families with immunoglobulin domains and cites prior work on adaptive immunity evolution.

claim: For gene families exclusive to bony vertebrates, there was enrichment of several sets of protein domains and functions including GPCR domain, lectin C-type domain, and C2H2-type zinc finger proteins.
source: For gene families exclusive to bony vertebrates (including the 414 gene families derived in the MRCA of bony vertebrates and 366 gene families lost in cartilaginous fishes), we found several enriched sets of protein domains and functions including GPCR domain, lectin C-type domain, and C2H2-type zinc finger proteins (Supplementary files 10 and 11).
evidence: The manuscript reports functional enrichment analysis results for bony vertebrate-specific gene families.

claim: The enrichment of GPCR protein function is consistent with the relative paucity of these receptors in cartilaginous fishes.
source: This enrichment of GPCR protein function is consistent with the relative paucity of these receptors in cartilaginous fishes, noted previously (Marra et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the GPCR enrichment finding with reference to prior work.

claim: Many of the GPCRs gained in the MRCA of bony vertebrates were olfactory receptors.
source: We found many of the GPCRs gained in the MRCA of bony vertebrates were olfactory receptors, which is also consistent with the relatively low number of olfactory receptors noted in cartilaginous fishes previously (Hara et al., 2018; Marra et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript reports the types of GPCRs gained and cites prior work on olfactory receptors in cartilaginous fishes.

claim: No orthologs of the NK gene cluster were found in cartilaginous fishes.
source: Among the lectin C-type domain proteins, we found no orthologs of the NK gene cluster in cartilaginous fishes (e.g. CD69, KLRC), a conserved complex of genes found across bony vertebrates, which implies potential differences in the natural killer complex in cartilaginous fishes (Kelley et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of NK gene cluster orthologs in cartilaginous fishes.

claim: 43 putative NLRs were identified in the whale shark.
source: We identified 43 putative NLRs in the whale shark.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of NLRs identified.

claim: Direct orthologs of almost all human NLRs were found in the whale shark.
source: We found direct orthologs of almost all human NLRs (UFBOOT=100 for all; Supplementary file 12), of which 23 contained a clearly identifiable NACHT domain (a signature of NLRs) (NOD1, NOD2, CIITA, NLRC5, NLRC3) while other putative orthologs did not (NLRX1, NLRC4, BIRC1, NWD1, TEP-1, and NLRP).
evidence: The manuscript reports the identification of human NLR orthologs in whale shark.

claim: Three orthologs of NOD1 were found in the whale shark.
source: Surprisingly, we found three orthologs of NOD1 in the whale shark, which is a key receptor for detection of intracellular bacteria, rather than a single copy as in humans (ultrafast bootstrap support, UFBOOT=100; Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of three NOD1 copies in whale shark.

claim: The three NOD1 copies resulted from tandem duplication events in the ancestor of cartilaginous fishes.
source: Further analyses intimate that the three NOD1 copies resulted from tandem duplication events in the ancestor of cartilaginous fishes (Appendix 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the evolutionary origin of the three NOD1 copies.

claim: All three of the whale shark NOD1s possess a canonical NACHT domain.
source: Sequence characterization suggests that all three of the whale shark NOD1s possess a canonical NACHT domain and so should retain a NOD1-like binding mechanism, but may have unique recognition specificity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Appendix 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports domain analysis of the three NOD1 copies.

claim: No NACHT domain containing orthologs of any of the 14 human NLRP genes were found in whale shark.
source: In contrast to the scenario observed for NOD1, we did not find NACHT domain containing orthologs of any of the 14 human NLRP genes, many of which activate inflammatory responses (Schroder and Tschopp, 2010), in whale shark, and only a single sequence lacking a detectable NACHT domain (Supplementary file 12, Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Appendix 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of NLRP orthologs in whale shark.

claim: A novel jawed vertebrate NLR gene family that appears to be closely related to the NLRPs was identified.
source: However, we did identify an apparently novel jawed vertebrate NLR gene family that appears to be closely related to the NLRPs (UFBOOT=67; Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of a novel NLR gene family.

claim: This novel NLR family has undergone significant expansion in the whale shark.
source: This family has undergone significant expansion in the whale shark (UFBOOT=100; Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and we tentatively suggest that this may compensate for the paucity of true NLRPs in whale shark.
evidence: The manuscript reports the expansion of the novel NLR family in whale shark.

claim: The NLR-based inflammasomes in humans and whale sharks are not directly orthologous.
source: Nonetheless, these results imply that the NLR-based inflammasomes in humans and whale sharks are not directly orthologous, and hence that NLR-based induction of inflammation and inflammation-induced programmed cell death (Schroder and Tschopp, 2010) are functionally distinct in human and whale shark.
evidence: The manuscript infers functional differences based on NLR repertoire differences.

claim: Each of the vertebrate species examined (human, zebrafish, and whale shark) has independently expanded different NLR subfamilies relative to the other species.
source: Interestingly, each of the vertebrate species we examined (human, zebrafish, and whale shark) has independently expanded different NLR subfamilies relative to the other species included in the analysis, with NLRP genes expanded in human (clade UFBOOT=99; Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and the previously identified 'fish-specific' FISNA in zebrafish (clade UFBOOT=86; Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports lineage-specific NLR expansions.

claim: A whale shark ortholog of the 'fish-specific' FISNA was found, suggesting this gene was present in the jawed vertebrate ancestor and is not a teleost novelty.
source: For the latter, we unexpectedly found a whale shark ortholog (UFBOOT=74), suggesting this gene was present in the jawed vertebrate ancestor and is not a teleost novelty.
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of FISNA ortholog in whale shark and infers its evolutionary origin.

claim: Multiple, independent NLR repertoire expansions have occurred during jawed vertebrate evolution despite the presence of the adaptive immune system.
source: In all, while we found evidence for a core set of NLRs in jawed vertebrates, our analyses also show that multiple, independent NLR repertoire expansions, with probable immunological relevance, have occurred during jawed vertebrate evolution despite the presence of the adaptive immune system.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the NLR evolution findings.

claim: Orthologs of each of the three canonical vertebrate RLRs (RIG-1, MDA5, and LGP2) exist in whale shark.
source: Our phylogenetic analyses of DEAD-Helicase and CARD domains indicate that orthologs of each of these genes exist in whale shark, revealing that all three RLRs had already diverged in the last common ancestor of extant jawed vertebrates (UFBOOT values all 100; Table 1, Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 12, Appendix 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the identification of all three RLR orthologs in whale shark.

claim: All three RLRs had already diverged in the last common ancestor of extant jawed vertebrates.
source: Our phylogenetic analyses of DEAD-Helicase and CARD domains indicate that orthologs of each of these genes exist in whale shark, revealing that all three RLRs had already diverged in the last common ancestor of extant jawed vertebrates (UFBOOT values all 100; Table 1, Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 12, Appendix 3).
evidence: The manuscript infers the evolutionary timing of RLR divergence.

claim: MDA5 and LGP2 are the result of a vertebrate-specific duplication, while RIG-1 split from these genes much earlier in animal evolution.
source: Further, and consistent with past findings (Mukherjee et al., 2014), we found that MDA5 and LGP2 are the result of a vertebrate-specific duplication, while RIG-1 split from these genes much earlier in animal evolution (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Appendix 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the evolutionary relationships of RLRs with reference to prior work.

claim: MAVS orthologs were identified in whale shark, elephant shark, and coelacanth.
source: We also identified MAVS orthologs in whale shark, elephant shark, and despite difficulties identifying a sequence previously (Boudinot et al., 2014), coelacanth (UFBOOT=100; Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 12, Appendix 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the identification of MAVS orthologs.

claim: The mammalian RLR repertoire (and MAVS) was established prior to the emergence of extant jawed vertebrates and has been highly conserved since.
source: These results show that the mammalian RLR repertoire (and MAVS) was established prior to the emergence of extant jawed vertebrates and has been highly conserved since, consistent with a lack of evidence for large RLR expansions in invertebrates.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the RLR evolution findings.

claim: 13 putative TLRs were identified in whale shark.
source: We identified 13 putative TLRs in whale shark (Supplementary file 12; Appendix 3), 11 of which are orthologous to TLR1/6/10, TLR2/28 (x2), TLR3, TLR7, TLR8, TLR9 (x2), TLR21, TLR22/23, and TLR27 (UFBOOT values all ≥99; Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Appendix 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of TLRs identified in whale shark.

claim: A novel ancestral jawed vertebrate TLR gene family related to TLR21, named TLR29, was discovered.
source: The remaining two, along with a coelacanth sequence, represent a novel ancestral jawed vertebrate TLR gene family related to TLR21, for which we propose the name TLR29 (UFBOOT = 99; Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of a new TLR family.

claim: The whale shark TLR repertoire is a unique combination when compared to all other vertebrates previously studied.
source: Thus, the whale shark TLR repertoire is a unique combination when compared to all other vertebrates previously studied, being formed from a mix of classic mammalian and teleost TLRs, supplemented with TLR27 and the new TLR29.
evidence: The manuscript characterizes the whale shark TLR repertoire.

claim: The ancestor of extant vertebrates possessed at least 15 TLRs.
source: Our rooted phylogenies indicate that the ancestor of extant vertebrates possessed at least 15 TLRs, while the ancestor of jawed vertebrates possessed at least 19 TLRs (including three distinct TLR9 lineages), both of which are larger repertoires than possessed by modern 2R species (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Appendix 3).
evidence: The manuscript infers the ancestral TLR repertoire size.

claim: The ancestor of jawed vertebrates possessed at least 19 TLRs (including three distinct TLR9 lineages).
source: Our rooted phylogenies indicate that the ancestor of extant vertebrates possessed at least 15 TLRs, while the ancestor of jawed vertebrates possessed at least 19 TLRs (including three distinct TLR9 lineages), both of which are larger repertoires than possessed by modern 2R species (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Appendix 3).
evidence: The manuscript infers the ancestral jawed vertebrate TLR repertoire size.

claim: Lineage-specific diversification of jawed vertebrate TLRs primarily resulted from differential loss (as well as genome duplications), supplemented by occasional gene duplication events.
source: Unlike invertebrates, where both loss and expansion of TLRs have been extensive, our data suggest that many jawed vertebrate TLRs existed in the jawed vertebrate ancestor, with lineage-specific diversification of jawed vertebrate TLRs primarily resulting from differential loss (as well as genome duplications), supplemented by occasional gene duplication events.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the TLR evolution findings.

claim: The jawed vertebrate ancestor possessed a core set of PRRs that has largely shaped the PRR repertoires of modern jawed vertebrates.
source: Overall, our findings imply that the jawed vertebrate ancestor possessed a core set of PRRs that has largely shaped the PRR repertoires of modern jawed vertebrates.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the PRR evolution findings.

claim: Adaptive immunity in gnathostomes did not fully displace germline-encoded PRR innovation.
source: We studied vertebrate pathogen recognition receptors (PRRs), which are key in initiating innate immune defense, and found diverse patterns of gene family evolution, demonstrating that adaptive immunity in gnathostomes did not fully displace germline-encoded PRR innovation.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding in the abstract.

claim: Substitution rates across a set of single-copy orthologs varied across vertebrate genomes, and these rates were relatively low in the whale shark compared to most other vertebrates.
source: Substitution rates across a set of single-copy orthologs varied across vertebrate genomes, and these rates were relatively low in the whale shark compared to most other vertebrates (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports substitution rate analysis results.

claim: Cartilaginous fishes have a significantly slower rate of substitution than bony vertebrates.
source: We also found that cartilaginous fishes have a significantly slower rate of substitution (p = 0.0004).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of the two-cluster test.

claim: Callorhinchus milii was found to be significantly slower in substitution rate than sharks.
source: In addition, C. milii (p = 0.0004) was found to be significantly slower than sharks, consistent with prior work (Weber et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of the two-cluster test comparing C. milii to sharks.

claim: The whale shark was not significantly different in substitution rate compared to the brownbanded bamboo shark.
source: The whale shark was not significantly different in rate compared to the brownbanded bamboo shark (p = 0.1802), its closest relative included in the analysis.
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of the two-cluster test comparing whale shark to bamboo shark.

claim: Cartilaginous fishes had a lower rate of molecular evolution compared to ray-finned fishes, sarcopterygians, the coelacanth, and tetrapods, but not significantly slower than the spotted gar.
source: We also found that cartilaginous fishes had a lower rate of molecular evolution compared to subsets of bony vertebrates including ray-finned fishes (p = 0.0004), sarcopterygians (p = 0.001), the coelacanth (p = 0.0004), and tetrapods (p = 0.0088), but not significantly slower than the spotted gar (p = 0.1416).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of multiple two-cluster tests.

claim: Chondrichthyan and giant vertebrate genomes had decreased substitution rates compared to other vertebrates.
source: We found chondrichthyan and giant vertebrate genomes had decreased substitution rates compared to other vertebrates, but gene family expansion rates varied among vertebrate giants, suggesting substitution and expansion rates of gene families are decoupled in vertebrate genomes.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding in the abstract.

claim: Gigantism in whale shark corresponds to a discrete shift in the rate of body size evolution to five times the background rate in cartilaginous fishes.
source: Consistent with previous research (Pimiento et al., 2019), we found that gigantism in whale shark corresponds to a discrete shift in the rate of body size evolution to five times the background rate in cartilaginous fishes (Appendix 4; Appendix 4—figure 1; Pimiento et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of body size evolution rate analysis.

claim: The model where rates of amino acid substitution leading to vertebrate giants differ from other vertebrates was significantly different than the strict clock.
source: Using PAML to fit models where the rates of amino acid substitution leading to vertebrate giants to other vertebrates differed, we found this model was significantly different than the strict clock (log-likelihood ratio test p = 1.76 × 10−56), indicating a significantly different rate of molecular substitution in vertebrate giants.
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of PAML analysis.

claim: Larger-bodied taxa have lower rates of protein evolution.
source: This finding is consistent with earlier evidence that larger-bodied taxa have lower rates of protein evolution (Martin and Palumbi, 1993).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on the relationship between body size and protein evolution rates.

claim: The rate of gene family size evolution in giant vertebrates was significantly faster than in the remaining branches, roughly double the rate in non-giant lineages.
source: We found that the rate of gene family size evolution in giant vertebrates was significantly faster than in the remaining branches, roughly double the rate in non-giant lineages (p < 0.002).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of CAFE analysis.

claim: Rates of gene family size evolution vary across all taxa including giant lineages, and an increase in gene family size evolution is not a consistent result of gigantism.
source: Mean change in gene family size shows that rates of gene family size evolution vary across all taxa including giant lineages, and that an increase in gene family size evolution is not a consistent result of gigantism.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the gene family size evolution rate data.

claim: The relationship of gigantism on gene substitution rates do not necessarily predict other forms of genomic evolution, including rates of gene family size evolution.
source: These results suggested that the relationship of gigantism on gene substitution rates do not necessarily predict other forms of genomic evolution, including rates of gene family size evolution.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the relationship between substitution rates and gene family size evolution rates.

claim: Substitution and expansion rates of gene families are decoupled in vertebrate genomes.
source: We found chondrichthyan and giant vertebrate genomes had decreased substitution rates compared to other vertebrates, but gene family expansion rates varied among vertebrate giants, suggesting substitution and expansion rates of gene families are decoupled in vertebrate genomes.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding in the abstract.

claim: 1387 gene families had a rate shift in gene family size evolution on at least one branch in the vertebrate phylogeny.
source: We inferred that 1387 gene families had a rate shift in gene family size evolution on at least one branch in the vertebrate phylogeny (at p < 0.05, Supplementary file 13).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of gene families with rate shifts.

claim: No gene families independently shifted in all giant taxa exclusive of other vertebrates.
source: No gene families independently shifted in all giant taxa exclusive of other vertebrates, and only five gene families independently shifted in any giant taxa exclusive of other branches in the vertebrate phylogeny (Supplementary file 13).
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of gene families with consistent shifts across all giants.

claim: Gene families that shifted in rates of gene gain and loss anywhere in vertebrate phylogeny were enriched for human orthologs in the Cancer Gene Census.
source: Interestingly, the gene families that shifted in rates of gene gain and loss anywhere in vertebrate phylogeny were also enriched for human orthologs in the Cancer Gene Census (Fisher's exact test, odds ratio = 1.43, p = 0.00414) (Sondka et al., 2018), suggesting that these cancer-relevant gene families were also more likely to shift in their expansion/contraction rate across vertebrates.
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of enrichment analysis for cancer genes.

claim: Gene families that shifted in expansion rate in vertebrate giants were enriched for human cancer-related genes.
source: Finally, we found gene families that shifted in expansion rate in vertebrate giants were enriched for human cancer-related genes, consistent with gigantism requiring adaptations to suppress cancer.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding in the abstract.

claim: Gene families that shifted along a branch leading to a vertebrate giant were enriched for cancer genes relative to all gene families that shifted in any branch in the vertebrate phylogeny.
source: Here, we found that these 1043 gene families were enriched for cancer genes relative to all gene families that shifted in any branch in the vertebrate phylogeny (odds ratio = 2.66, p = 0.00199), with over twice as many cancer-related gene families estimated to have shifted in rate among all vertebrate lineages than the null expectation.
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of enrichment analysis for cancer genes in giant branches.

claim: Gene families that shifted along branches leading to the non-giant vertebrates sister to the giant vertebrates were not significantly enriched for cancer gene families.
source: For comparison, we also did the same test but focusing on any gene families that shifted along branches leading to the non-giant vertebrates sister to the giant vertebrates (i.e. brownbanded bamboo shark, pufferfishes, hyrax, bottlenose dolphin), and found that there was no significant enrichment for cancer gene families along those branches (odds ratio = 0.88, p = 0.624).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of enrichment analysis for cancer genes in non-giant sister branches.

claim: The observed odds ratio of 2.66 for cancer gene enrichment in giant branches was more extreme than 98% of random odds ratios.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed the significance of the observed effect size by randomly drawing sets of branches across the vertebrate phylogeny to test for enrichment of cancer genes along random sets of branches, and found that the observed odds ratio of 2.66 was more extreme than 98% of random odds ratios (i.e. p = 0.02).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of permutation test.

claim: There was a significantly higher rate of gene family size evolution along branches leading to giant taxa vs. other branches.
source: By fitting a linear mixed model using lme4, we found that there was a significantly higher rate of gene family size evolution along branches leading to giant taxa vs. other branches (coefficient 0.0203, p = 5.95e−6), no effect of whether a gene was related to cancer on rates (coefficient −0.00245, p = 0.219), but a significant interaction of cancer suppression function and gigantism (coefficient 0.0102, p = 8.51e−5), such that rates of gene family size evolution in genes related to cancer leading to giant taxa are even higher than expected relative to the effect of being on a giant branch alone (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of linear mixed model analysis.

claim: In gene families where a rate shift occurred, the mean rate of gene family size evolution along branches leading to giant taxa was 3.32 times greater than the mean rate along other branches in cancer genes.
source: In these gene families where a rate shift occurred, we found the mean rate of gene family size evolution along branches leading to giant taxa was 3.32 times greater than the mean rate along other branches in cancer genes, but branches leading to giant taxa had only an average rate that was 2.60 times greater than other branches in genes not related to cancer.
evidence: The manuscript reports the comparison of rate ratios between cancer and non-cancer genes.

claim: Dynamics of vertebrate evolution in cancer-related gene family size among the sampled taxa are driven by the evolution of gigantism.
source: Overall, this is suggestive that dynamics of vertebrate evolution in cancer-related gene family size among the sampled taxa are driven by the evolution of gigantism.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the relationship between gigantism and cancer gene family size evolution.

claim: Larger-bodied organisms tend to have lower cancer rates than expected given their increased numbers of cells relative to smaller-bodied organisms.
source: Larger-bodied organisms tend to have lower cancer rates than expected given their increased numbers of cells relative to smaller-bodied organisms (Peto et al., 1975), suggesting genes involved in cancer suppression may evolve differently in vertebrate giants.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on Peto's paradox.

claim: Recent research in giant mammals such as elephants and whales has identified selection or duplication of various gene families that are related to suppressing cancer in humans.
source: Recent research in giant mammals such as elephants and whales supports this hypothesis and has identified selection or duplication of various gene families that are related to suppressing cancer in humans (Abegglen et al., 2015; Sulak et al., 2016; Tollis et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on cancer suppression in giant mammals.

claim: The duplication of tumor suppressor protein TP53 has been implicated in reduced cancer rates in proboscideans (elephants and relatives) relative to other mammals.
source: Cancer suppression has evolved by different mechanisms across mammalian lineages, including gene family expansions (Tollis et al., 2017); for example, the duplication of tumor suppressor protein TP53 has been implicated in reduced cancer rates in proboscideans (elephants and relatives) relative to other mammals (Sulak et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on TP53 duplication in elephants.

claim: TP53 is not expanded in baleen whales.
source: By contrast, this same gene family is not expanded in baleen whales (Tollis et al., 2017), thus it is already known the same gene families do not expand in all mammalian giants, so we should not expect this to be the case when including fishes.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on TP53 in baleen whales.

claim: A rate shift in gene family size evolution in TP53 was confirmed in the lineage leading to elephant.
source: We confirmed a rate shift in gene family size evolution in TP53 in the lineage leading to elephant, but this gene family also had a rate shift for TP53 along the branch leading to minke whale (but not bowhead whale), as well as the non-giant bamboo shark.
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of gene family size evolution analysis for TP53.

claim: Cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) are fundamental for understanding vertebrate evolution.
source: Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fishes) are fundamental for understanding vertebrate evolution, yet their genomes are understudied.
evidence: The manuscript states this in the abstract.

claim: Jawed vertebrates (Gnathostomata) comprise two extant major groups, the cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) and the bony vertebrates (Osteichthyes, including Tetrapoda).
source: Jawed vertebrates (Gnathostomata) comprise two extant major groups, the cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) and the bony vertebrates (Osteichthyes, including Tetrapoda) (Venkatesh et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: Callorhinchus milii separated from the Elasmobranchii (sharks, rays, and skates) approximately 420 million years ago.
source: As a member of the Holocephali (chimaeras, ratfishes), one of the two major groups of cartilaginous fishes, C. milii separated from the Elasmobranchii (sharks, rays, and skates) ~420 million years ago, shortly after the divergence from bony vertebrates.
evidence: The manuscript states the divergence time.

claim: The whale shark (Rhincodon typus) is by far the largest of all extant fishes, reaching a maximum confirmed length of nearly 19 m.
source: Famously representing one of Earth's ocean giants, the whale shark is by far the largest of all extant fishes, reaching a maximum confirmed length of nearly 19 m (McClain et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on whale shark size.

claim: The first draft elasmobranch genome published was for a male whale shark of Taiwanese origin by Read et al., 2017.
source: The first draft elasmobranch genome published was for a male whale shark of Taiwanese origin by Read et al., 2017.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on whale shark genome.

claim: A toll-like receptor (TLR) similar to TLR21 was found in the first whale shark genome draft assembly.
source: A toll-like receptor (TLR) similar to TLR21 was also found in this first whale shark genome draft assembly, suggesting that TLR21 was derived in the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of jawed vertebrates.
evidence: The manuscript refers to a finding from the first whale shark genome.

claim: Long-read sequencing is an important factor in assembling longer contigs to resolve repetitive regions which comprise the majority of vertebrate genomes.
source: Long-read sequencing is an important factor in assembling longer contigs to resolve repetitive regions which comprise the majority of vertebrate genomes (Koren et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on the importance of long-read sequencing.

claim: The scaffolded whale shark genome had 39,176 scaffolds and a scaffold N50 of 344,460 bp.
source: The scaffolded genome had 39,176 scaffolds and a scaffold N50 of 344,460 bp.
evidence: The manuscript reports scaffolded assembly statistics.

claim: Branchiostoma is notable among animals for retaining a relatively high number of gene families present in the animal stem branch.
source: Although accurate inference of gene family size evolution in vertebrates may benefit from further taxon sampling among invertebrates, Branchiostoma is notable among animals for retaining a relatively high number of gene families present in the animal stem branch (Richter et al., 2018), hence it is one of the best outgroup species to vertebrates to study the origins of novel genes within the vertebrate clade.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on Branchiostoma gene families.

claim: Cartilaginous fishes are the most distant evolutionarily lineage relative to humans to possess both an adaptive and innate immune system.
source: Given that cartilaginous fishes are the most distant evolutionarily lineage relative to humans to possess both an adaptive and innate immune system, the study of their PRR repertoire is important to understanding the integration of the two systems in early jawed vertebrates.
evidence: The manuscript states this phylogenetic relationship.

claim: Several deuterostome invertebrate genomes possess greater expanded PRR repertoires when compared to relatively conserved repertoires found in bony vertebrates.
source: For example, previous work has shown several deuterostome invertebrate genomes possess greater expanded PRR repertoires when compared to relatively conserved repertoires found in bony vertebrates, which suggests that adaptive immunity may have negated the need for many new PRRs in jawed vertebrates (Huang et al., 2008; Rast et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2013), although this hypothesis has not been formally tested.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on PRR repertoires in invertebrates and vertebrates.

claim: Adaptive immunity may have negated the need for many new PRRs in jawed vertebrates.
source: For example, previous work has shown several deuterostome invertebrate genomes possess greater expanded PRR repertoires when compared to relatively conserved repertoires found in bony vertebrates, which suggests that adaptive immunity may have negated the need for many new PRRs in jawed vertebrates (Huang et al., 2008; Rast et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2013), although this hypothesis has not been formally tested.
evidence: The manuscript cites a hypothesis from prior work.

claim: NLRs are intracellular receptors that detect a wide array of pathogen- (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs).
source: NLRs are intracellular receptors that detect a wide array of pathogen- (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) (e.g. flagellin, extracellular ATP, glucose) (Fritz and Kufer, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about NLR function.

claim: RLRs are intracellular receptors that detect viral nucleic acid and initiate immune responses through mitochondrial antiviral signaling (MAVS) protein.
source: RLRs are intracellular receptors that detect viral nucleic acid and initiate immune responses through mitochondrial antiviral signaling (MAVS) protein (Mukherjee et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about RLR function.

claim: Bony vertebrates have three RLRs: RIG-1 (encoded by DDX58), MDA5 (IFIH1), and LGP2 (DHX58).
source: Bony vertebrates have three RLRs: RIG-1 (encoded by DDX58), MDA5 (IFIH1), and LGP2 (DHX58).
evidence: The manuscript states established knowledge about RLRs in bony vertebrates.

claim: TLRs recognize a wide variety of PAMPs and are probably the best known of all innate immune receptors.
source: TLRs recognize a wide variety of PAMPs and are probably the best known of all innate immune receptors.
evidence: The manuscript states established knowledge about TLR function.

claim: Large expansions of TLRs have been observed in several invertebrate lineages.
source: While large expansions have been observed in several invertebrate lineages (Huang et al., 2008; Rast et al., 2006), many studies suggest that the vertebrate TLR repertoire is largely conserved (Boudinot et al., 2014; Braasch et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on TLR expansions in invertebrates.

claim: Many studies suggest that the vertebrate TLR repertoire is largely conserved.
source: While large expansions have been observed in several invertebrate lineages (Huang et al., 2008; Rast et al., 2006), many studies suggest that the vertebrate TLR repertoire is largely conserved (Boudinot et al., 2014; Braasch et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on TLR conservation in vertebrates.

claim: TLR expansion in codfishes is due to a proposed loss of CD4 and MHC class II.
source: Some teleosts appear to be an exception to this rule; however, this is likely due to the teleost-specific whole-genome duplication, and loss of CD4 and MHC class II in codfishes (Solbakken et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on TLR expansion in codfishes.
